Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.finding: The protagonist of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928): born 1875, a pre-revolutionary district marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства) from Stargorod, reduced after 1917 to a clerk registering marriages and deaths at the local ZAGS; a 52-year-old widower whose childhood nickname 'Kisa' Ostap Bender gleefully adopts along with mock titles ('field marshal', 'giant of thought'). For a Russian reader the name is a byword for the proud, helpless, faintly ridiculous ex-gentleman of the NEP years, and its alternation between 'Vorobyaninov' and 'Ippolit Matveyevich' is part of the deadpan mock-solemn narration. English coverage is settled: Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation, the 1961 Richardson translation and English Wikipedia all use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov' ('Vorobianinov' is a rare Library-of-Congress-style variant). Chinese translations (Zhang Peiwen, People's Literature 2004; Bai Huaxiong; Xu Changhan, Jiangsu Phoenix 2022) consistently write the surname 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, with the given name as 伊坡利 in older editions and 伊波利特 as the standard modern transliteration of Ippolit. Japanese film and review pages use ヴォロビヤニノフ; Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969 Shueisha translation used the older ボロビヤニノフ (イポリット・マトベイッチ).

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃洛比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: Russian narration alternates surname (Vorobyaninov) with name-plus-patronymic (Ippolit Matveyevich); both refer to the same man, and Bender's 'Kisa' is his childhood pet name.
Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.rationale: Denotation and the surname/name-patronymic alternation are kept in all three languages, using the spelling already established in each (Fisher/Wikipedia for English, the three Chinese translations' 沃洛比亚尼诺夫, the modern Japanese ヴォ- form); the fixed spelling is bound once and never collapsed to a single form. Given up: the connotation that 'Ippolit Matveyevich' is a respectful formal address while the bare surname is dry narratorial distance, which only a one-line note can supply to a non-Russian reader.

гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.finding: Bezenchuk is the drunken coffin-maker of the town of N in chapter 1 ('Безенчук и «нимфы»'): he stands at the door of his 'потасканное заведение', competes with the funeral bureau «Нимфа» (a third firm, «Милости просим», has already gone bust), boasts 'у нас что ни гроб — то огурчик', classifies deaths by rank, and swears 'туды его в качель'; Ilf took the surname from the railway station Bezenchuk near Samara. 'Гробовых дел мастер' is the pre-revolutionary guild formula (cf. 'золотых дел мастер' = goldsmith, 'часовых дел мастер') applied to coffins, so the epithet is a mock-solemn craft title, not a plain job name; the authors repeat it as a set formula, and it has since become a stock ironic phrase (Mokienko-Nikitina record it in 2000s school slang as a joke name for the shop teacher). Existing renderings: John Richardson (1961) flattens it to 'the undertaker'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern UP, 2011) keeps the title as 'master coffin-maker Bezenchuk'. Chinese editions use 棺材匠别津丘克 (WeRead edition; chapter title 别津丘克和'山林女神') or 别赞丘克 (Zhang Peiwen, 2004). The Japanese translation by 江川卓 (1966/1969) exists but I could not find its wording for the epithet online.

rendering.ja: 棺桶細工の親方ベゼンチューク

гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.note_for_reader: 'Master coffin-maker' mimics the old Russian guild title (as in 'goldsmith', lit. 'master of gold affairs'); the authors use it as a running mock-solemn epithet.
гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.rationale: All three keep the denotation (he makes coffins, he is not the Nymph funeral bureau) and the connotation of a craft-guild title through a 'master' word (master / 师傅 / 親方), with the formula repeated verbatim each time so the joke stays a refrain; what is given up is the archaic genitive-plural syntax of 'X-ых дел', which none of the target languages can echo without sounding like a mistranslation. English follows Fisher's established rendering; Chinese adds 师傅 to the established 棺材匠; Japanese is a new rendering because the Egawa wording could not be verified.

«Нимфа».finding: «Нимфа» is the fictional rival funeral parlour in the district town of N (Stargorod) in chapter I of «Двенадцать стульев», whose title is «Безенчук и „нимфы“»: «По левую руку за волнистыми зеленоватыми стеклами серебрились гробы похоронного бюро „Нимфа“», run by three co-owners the narrator calls its «нимфы». The joke for a Russian reader is the pretentious Greek-mythological trade name (a NEP-era private firm aping pre-revolutionary chic) hung on a coffin shop, and Bezenchuk's contemptuous refrain «Разве „Нимфа“, туды ее в качель, товар дает?» against his own defunct «Милости просим». Established English coverage renders it as the Nymph: Richardson (1961) has 'the Nymph Funeral Home' / 'Does the Nymph, durn it, really give good service?' and Fisher (2011, Northwestern) titles the chapter 'Bezenchuk and the Nymphs'. Chinese editions are split: 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) '别赞丘克与“自然女神”', 徐昌翰 (后浪 2022) '别津丘克和“山林女神”', 白桦熊 (上海译文) '别津丘克与“仙女”'; none uses the transliteration 宁芙. The Japanese 江川卓 translation (集英社 1966/1969) is not available online, so its rendering could not be checked.
«Нимфа».note_for_reader: «Нимфа» (the Nymph) is the grandly named private funeral parlour that competes with Bezenchuk; a Greek nymph on a coffin shop is the joke.
«Нимфа».rationale: All three keep the denotation (one recognisable firm name, consistent across chapters) and the mock-classical connotation; English follows the established Richardson/Fisher form with 'the Nymph Funeral Home' on first mention, Japanese uses the familiar loanword in 「」 with 葬儀店 on first mention, and Chinese takes the existing plain 仙女 (add 殡仪馆 on first mention) over the opaque transliteration 宁芙, giving up the specifically Greek flavour for instant legibility of the joke.

гробовых дел мастер.finding: Not a real trade name: it is the narrator's mock-solemn coinage on the archaic sign-board formula '-ых дел мастер' (часовых дел мастер = watchmaker, золотых дел мастер = goldsmith, заплечных дел мастер = executioner; all marked устар. in the Malyi akademicheskii slovar), applied deadpan to Bezenchuk, a hard-drinking NEP-era private artisan whose 'dusty, boring oak coffins' sit in the window on Comrade Gubernsky Street (ch. 1, 'Безенчук и нимфы'). The pompous title, set against his shabby shop and his rival firm 'Nymph', is the joke; plain гробовщик would carry none of it. The phrase became a catchphrase: Mokienko and Nikitina's Большой словарь русских поговорок (2007) records 'гробовых дел мастер' as school slang, шутл.-ирон., for a shop teacher (attested 2003), and the 1971/1976 films fixed 'гробовых дел мастер Безенчук' in popular memory. Existing translations split: John Richardson (1961, lib.ru) flattens it to 'Bezenchuk, the undertaker'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) keeps the title as 'master coffin-maker Bezenchuk'. The Chinese translation by 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2021) uses plain '棺材匠别津丘克' alongside '别津丘克师傅'; the Japanese translation (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) exists but I could not verify its wording online, so the ja rendering is a choice, not an established one.
sources: https://www.amazon.co.jp/十二の椅子-1969年-イリヤ・イリフ/dp/B000J94TF4
гробовых дел мастер.note_for_reader: A mock guild title on the pattern of 'master watchmaker'; the plain word for the trade is гробовщик, which the narrator pointedly avoids.
гробовых дел мастер.rationale: All three keep the guild-rank word (master / 匠师 / 親方) so the deadpan pomp survives and the term stays distinct from plain 'coffin-maker / 棺材匠 / 棺桶屋'; en binds Fisher's established rendering. What is given up is the archaic sign-board syntax of '-ых дел', which has no living equivalent in any of the three languages.

стол регистрации смертей и браков.finding: In the 1928 text the phrase is 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков': contrary to the brief, the book does name the загс (ЗАГС, отдел записи актов гражданского состояния), the Soviet civil registry created by the decree of 18 Dec 1917 that made civil marriage the only legally valid one and moved births, marriages and deaths from church metrical books to state offices, so Vorobyaninov, a former marshal of the nobility, now keeps the very ledgers the Church used to keep. 'Стол' here is the old Russian bureaucratic unit (a 'desk' or section of an office) and also the literal desk, which the narrator then says looks like an old gravestone gnawed by rats; the joke rests on the deaths-first word order and on a nobleman reduced to a clerkship. For a Russian reader the term reads as deadpan office jargon, faintly pre-revolutionary (столоначальник) and therefore ironic. Richardson's 1961 English has 'he worked in the registry office, where he was in charge of the registration of deaths and marriages'; the 1966 Egawa Japanese speaks of him as 登記所に勤める; no Chinese rendering of the exact phrase could be located online (the 白桦熊 edition is paywalled), so the zh choice is unattested.
стол регистрации смертей и браков.note_for_reader: ZAGS: the Soviet civil registry that replaced church record-keeping after 1917; render the office itself as 'the civil registry office' / 民事登记处 / 戸籍登録所 wherever загс appears.
стол регистрации смертей и браков.rationale: Kept denotation (a civil, not church, desk) and the deaths-before-marriages order that carries the comedy, and kept 'desk/台/窓口' so the gravestone-desk image two sentences later still lands; gave up the faint tsarist столоначальник flavour of 'стол' as an office unit, which no target language reproduces, and, in Chinese, used the natural 登记台 over the literal 桌.

картуз.finding: A картуз is a soft civilian cap with a flat round crown on a stiff band and a hard visor — a фуражка stripped of cockade, piping and every uniform element; the word came from Dutch karpoets ('travel cap') via Peter's time and by the late 19th century was the standard summer headgear of peasants, urban craftsmen, factory workers and small tradesmen. In 1928 it still marked its wearer as 'simple people' as against the hats of the former gentry and the caps (кепки) of the new Soviet youth, which is exactly why the coffin-maker Bezenchuk is drawn with one: he presses it to his chest before 'господин Воробьянинов' (chapter II, 'прижимая к груди картуз') and later goes home 'балансируя картузом'. John Richardson's English renders it simply 'cap'; the standard dictionary equivalent (Wiktionary, bab.la) is 'peaked cap'; Zhang Peiwen's People's Literature translation uses 便帽 (别赞丘克把便帽扣在胸前); the Russian–Japanese dictionary on Kotobank glosses it 前びさしの硬い男性用帽子, and I could not verify the wording of Egawa Taku's 1969 Chikuma translation. Note: the prompt's instruction to look at coverage of 'Durov and VKontakte' is irrelevant to this term and was not followed.
картуз.note_for_reader: картуз: the stiff-visored cloth cap of Russian tradesmen and peasants, a civilian cousin of the uniform cap; it marks Bezenchuk as a small artisan.
картуз.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a visored cloth cap, not a hat) and the plain register; 'peaked cap' and 便帽 follow established dictionary/published usage and give up the class marking, which the one-line note restores, while 鳥打帽 (the Meiji-era merchant's cap) keeps the tradesman connotation at the cost of a slightly different silhouette — chosen over the modern, sporty 鸭舌帽, which would read as anachronistic.

conventions: Dialogue dashes: render Russian em-dash dialogue as English double quotes, Chinese “” and Japanese 「」; never keep the dash in the target text. [rank 1]

Names: keep name+patronymic where the Russian has it, one fixed transliteration per language (en Library-of-Congress style without diacritics, zh standard 新华社 transliteration, ja katakana with ・ separators); no honorifics added in Japanese for narration. [rank 1]
ты/вы: Vorobyaninov addresses Bezenchuk as ты and is addressed as вы; render in Japanese as plain form vs です・ます, in Chinese as 你 vs 您, and in English through tone rather than pronouns. [rank 1]
Dialogue: the Russian em-dash lines become en double quotation marks, zh “ ”, ja 「 」; the narrator's deadpan asides stay in the same paragraph, never demoted to footnotes. [rank 2]

Names: transliterate (en BGN-style without diacritics, zh standard 新华社 forms, ja katakana with long vowels), keep name-plus-patronymic wherever the Russian uses it, and add no Japanese honorifics; 'мадам' stays 'Madame / 夫人 / マダム'. [rank 2]

Soviet acronyms and NEP institutions (страхкасса, ЗАГС etc.) are expanded into a short descriptive phrase inside the sentence; a translator's note only when no phrase conveys the joke; the Wikisource line 'Категория:...' at the end of page 5 is not text and is dropped. [rank 2]

Name-and-patronymic address is kept as in Russian (never replaced by surname or first name); one transliteration table per language (en: BGN-style with -yevich/-ovna; zh: Xinhua standard syllables; ja: katakana with long-vowel marks). [rank 3]
